documents: Jiang, González & Bürgmann, preprint 'Subduction earthquakes controlled by incoming plate geometry: The 2020 M>7.5 Shumagin, Alaska, earthquake doublet' (submitted to EPSL, dated November 24, 2021; PDF, 46 pages)

entry.evidence: the second event was unusual as it broke a trench-perpendicular fault within the incoming oceanic slab

sequences.source_document: Jiang, González & Bürgmann preprint (EarthArXiv, 24 Nov 2021), supplied as the published paper

steps.action: Took USGS and GCMT catalogue solutions showing a thrust M7.8 and a strike-slip M7.6, trench-parallel and trench-perpendicular aftershocks, and centroid depths of 30-35 km.
steps.quote: The focal mechanism solutions from the GCMT catalog suggest the mechanism of the M7.8 event is of thrust-faulting type

steps.action: Posed the aim: what controlled the rupture extent of the M7.8, the slab-tearing M7.6, and the interaction between them, given the Shumagin seismic-gap context.
steps.quote: We investigate the major controls for the 2020 Shumagin earthquake doublet.

steps.action: Assembled the record of both events: Nevada Geodetic Laboratory GNSS coseismic offsets and daily postseismic series, and six Sentinel-1 interferograms from three tracks processed with ISCE TopsApp; modelled and removed 48-day postseismic signal from the ascending M7.8 interferogram.
steps.quote: We used 12 European Space Agency Sentinel-1 satellite interferometric wide swath mode images

steps.action: Checked the InSAR record against a preseismic interferogram (atmospheric noise only, Fig. S1) and checked M7.6 interferograms for transient postseismic signals before deciding on corrections.
steps.quote: the interferometric phase is dominated by the turbulent atmosphere delays

steps.action: Applied the authors' earlier WGBIS Bayesian inversion of wrapped InSAR phase, which skips phase unwrapping across the island water gaps, to estimate uniform-slip fault geometry.
steps.quote: directly inverts for fault source parameters by applying the WGBIS method

steps.action: Extended WGBIS to distributed slip with a seven-parameter two-dimensional elliptical crack model adapted from the Ke et al. (2020) laboratory slip profile, as a physics-based regularization.
steps.quote: Next, we propose an extension to the WGBIS method

steps.action: Validated the elliptical-crack inversion with synthetic tests and compared its performance with other slip-inversion methods (Fig. S14, supplement).
steps.quote: We also design synthetic tests to validate our approach

steps.action: Inverted wrapped phase and GNSS for the M7.8 rectangular fault: 112±2 km long, 14-44 km depth, 1.5 m thrust slip, dip 26±0.5°, steeper than Slab2's ~15°.
steps.quote: the inferred fault geometry requires a relatively steep dip angle

steps.action: Repeated the geometry inversion with GNSS only, InSAR only and both data sets; all gave 25-28° dip.
steps.quote: In all cases, the obtained fault geometries are consistent with a

steps.action: Set two rival 3D interface geometries: a two-segment model (26° deep segment plus a shallow segment to the trench) and the Slab2 interface.
steps.quote: We tested two different 3D fault geometry parameterizations.

steps.action: Solved for elliptical-crack slip on each geometry; the proposed geometry fit GNSS with 97-99% variance reduction.
steps.quote: We solve for the slip distribution of the elliptical rupture model on our proposed fault geometry.

steps.action: Compared fits: GNSS fit comparably on both geometries, but InSAR wrapped-phase residual variance was 1.02 rad on Slab2 versus 0.87 rad on the proposed geometry, and Slab2 posteriors were less well resolved.
steps.quote: the variance of InSAR wrapped phase residuals is 1.02 rad (or 0.91 cm) for the inversion on the Slab2 geometry

steps.action: Rejected the Slab2 geometry for the M7.8 rupture in favour of the steeper two-segment geometry.
steps.quote: the distributed slip model on the Slab2 geometry cannot reproduce the InSAR surface displacement patterns as well

steps.action: Compared the final slip model (peak 1.8 m, Mw 7.79) with published seismic and geodetic slip models (Crowell & Melgar 2020; Ye et al. 2021); main slip area overlaps, details differ.
steps.quote: The rupture area with significant slip (>1.5m) is largely overlapped with the finite-fault slip model

steps.action: Inverted 89-day exponential-fit GNSS postseismic offsets with SDM (smoothing 0.3 from a trade-off curve) on an extended interface; found afterslip up-dip (6-14 km) and east and west of the rupture, Mw 7.60, and none below it.
steps.quote: the spatial distribution of postseismic slip is resolved by using the slip inversion package, SDM

steps.action: Compared the afterslip model with Crowell & Melgar (2020) and with Zhao et al. (pers. comm.); partial agreement.
steps.quote: The afterslip region east of the mainshock in their model is generally consistent with our afterslip model.

steps.action: Used aftershock alignment to parameterize the M7.6 and inverted for a right-lateral strike-slip fault, 19-39 km deep, N-S striking and east dipping, Mw 7.55, beneath the slab interface.
steps.quote: The coseismic slip model shows right-lateral strike-slip motion on a fault plane perpendicular to the Alaska subduction zone

steps.action: Checked the intraslab depth against independent aftershock depths: 70% of M2.5+ aftershocks lie at 20-40 km.
steps.quote: This is also confirmed from the focal depth range of the aftershocks.

steps.action: Ran synthetic experiments: uniform slip may overestimate dip by ~2.5° and top depth by ~2 km; layered versus homogeneous earth models change surface displacements by 2-50% (Supplementary Sections 3-4).
steps.quote: A synthetic experiment shows that, for the M7.8 earthquake, the inversion with rectangular uniform slip might lead to an overestimated dip

steps.action: Compared the inferred geometry with independent seismic reflection Line 4 (Li et al. 2015) and with the Crowell & Melgar (2020) GNSS-vertical grid search (25° dip).
steps.quote: The seismic reflectors are consistent with our inferred fault geometry.

steps.action: Proposed that megathrust dip changes (decollement-ramp structure, as in the 2015 Gorkha case of Hubbard et al. 2016) bounded the M7.8 rupture; the 14 km top depth matches reflection-imaged dip changes.
steps.quote: Our findings suggest that the fault geometry controls the rupture size and extent.

steps.action: Kept the claim that down-dip variation in fault orientation likely limited the M7.8 rupture extent.
steps.quote: the variation in fault orientation with depth was likely a controlling factor limiting the extent of the Shumagin rupture

steps.action: Back-rotated the M7.6 fault (strike 15°, dip 60°) and matched it to fabric from the Kula-Resurrection ridges, active 60-40 Ma (Fuston & Wu 2020).
steps.quote: This strike angle is consistent with the spreading of the Kula-Resurrection ridges

steps.action: Excluded trench-parallel outer-rise bending faults and Pacific-Kula or Pacific-Farallon ridge fabric as the M7.6 source, because their orientations do not match.
steps.quote: The pre-existing faults are unlikely to have formed along the Pacific-Kula ridge

steps.action: Checked the M7.6 location against a published upper-mantle low shear-velocity (hydration) anomaly (Li et al. 2020) and outer-rise P-wave reductions (Shillington et al. 2015).
steps.quote: our M7.6 fault model is correlated with the location of a low seismic-velocity anomaly

steps.action: Took Herman & Furlong's (2021) simulated right-lateral shear stress from lateral coupling variation, and qualified it with lower geodetic coupling estimates (Drooff & Freymueller 2021).
steps.quote: The lateral displacement variations can impose large-magnitude, right-lateral shear stresses on the M7.6 rupture plane geometry

steps.action: Computed Coulomb stress changes from M7.8 coseismic and postseismic slip on the extended M7.6 fault plane with Coulomb 3.3.
steps.quote: we calculate the stress perturbations on the M7.6 event

steps.action: Compared the stress change with the 0.01 MPa triggering threshold: coseismic shear +0.1 MPa and unclamping +0.3 MPa at the hypocentre, postseismic near-neutral; concluded the M7.6 was likely triggered by coseismic stress.
steps.quote: Our Coulomb stress models suggest that the second, M7.6 intraslab, earthquake was likely triggered

steps.action: Applied the same stress calculation to the 29 July 2021 M8.2 Semidi earthquake, which occurred while the paper was being written; positive shear changes from coseismic and postseismic slip.
steps.quote: This indicates that both M7.8 coseismic and postseismic slip on the megathrust interface could have triggered the M8.2 event.

steps.action: Concluded that the Shumagin gap is segmented: the M7.8 broke the eastern deep segment, the western and shallow parts remain unruptured hazards, and the M7.6 reactivated Kula-Resurrection fabric.
steps.quote: We propose that the Shumagin gap is segmented and has variable mechanical characteristics.

tree.answer: Yes: a doublet of a megathrust M7.8 and an intraslab strike-slip M7.6 in the Shumagin gap
No: fault geometry and slip are latent, inferred from surface deformation
Controls on rupture extent, gap segmentation and triggering
Steep two-segment interface vs Slab2; Kula-Resurrection fabric vs outer-rise or other ridge fabric
Yes for geometry: different InSAR wrapped-phase fits

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Partly: the 2021 M8.2 serves as a second case for the stress-transfer calculation
Yes: data subsets, synthetic bias tests, earth-model tests, independent reflection and aftershock data

end.claim: The Shumagin megathrust is segmented: the M7.8 ruptured a 26°-dipping deep segment (14-44 km) bounded up-dip by a bend to ~8°, and the segmented megathrust structure and intraslab faults (reactivated Kula-Resurrection fabric hosting the triggered M7.6) limited the rupture and segment the gap.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the wrapped-phase Bayesian (WGBIS) inversion yielding a 26° dip incompatible with Slab2, there would be no segmented-geometry claim.

gates.evidence: Data are routine satellite and GNSS acquisitions of a live event, not directed by a hypothesis (pp. 7-8). The steep geometry faced a fit test against Slab2 that it could have lost (p. 15), and the Coulomb calculation could have returned negative stress (p. 26), but the control-by-geometry and ridge-fabric claims rest on consistency arguments (pp. 22-24). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: elliptical crack and inclusion shape from plane elastostatics (Sendeckyj 1970)
analytical crack slip profile from a laboratory experiment (Ke et al. 2020)
Sentinel-1 SAR interferometry processed with ISCE

novelty_claims.quote: This is the first documented earthquake doublet involving a megathrust event and a strike-slip event.
to our knowledge, these earthquakes are the first documented sizable earthquake doublet to involve a megathrust earthquake rupture
applying a novel physics-based fault slip regularization

limits: The supplied document is the November 2021 EarthArXiv preprint, not the typeset EPSL article (DOI 10.1016/j.epsl.2022.117447). Its acknowledgments thank the editor and referees, so it is probably a revised version, but no review file was supplied and no review sequence is coded. The supplement (Figs. S1-S16, Sections 1-4) was not supplied; steps resting on it are coded from main-text descriptions. Sub-claims and their statuses: the M7.8 geometry and slip are estimate_with_resolution (26±0.5° dip, 14-44 km), though the authors concede the uncertainties are underestimated (pp. 19-21); the afterslip distribution is estimate_with_resolution; Coulomb triggering of the M7.6 is best_explanation; reactivation of Kula-Resurrection fabric for the M7.6 is best_explanation by exclusion on orientation only. The single reported failure is that two-segment M7.6 inversions were unstable, so a possible shallow trench-parallel segment (Lay 2021) remains unresolved (p. 19). Inference: the text does not show whether the slab-bend interpretation was formed before or after the inversion results, or whether other geometries or regularizations were tried and dropped. Comparisons with published slip models rely partly on a personal communication (Zhao et al.) and on conference talks (Lay 2021; Shillington 2021).

disagreements.target: Slab2 subduction interface model (Hayes et al., 2018)
disagreements.support: Wrapped-phase plus GNSS inversions give a 26° dip at 14-44 km against Slab2's ~15°; slip on the Slab2 geometry fits InSAR worse (1.02 vs 0.87 rad residual variance); seismic reflection Line 4 agrees with the steeper geometry.
disagreements.quote: substantially deviates from the most recent subduction interface model Slab2

disagreements.target: Moment tensor dip angles of 17-20° (Ye et al., 2021)
disagreements.support: Attributes the lower moment-tensor dip to moment-dip trade-off and dependence on assumed depth, while acknowledging its own dip uncertainty may be underestimated.
disagreements.quote: which is also lower than the dip angle retrieved from geodetic observations

disagreements.target: Finite-fault slip model of Ye et al. (2021)
disagreements.support: The main slip areas overlap, but the low-dimensional elliptical model gives one compact patch rather than two separated ruptures plus several small patches.
disagreements.quote: while our rupture model preferred a wider and compact slip distribution

disagreements.target: Early afterslip model of Crowell and Melgar (2020)
disagreements.support: Their model places most afterslip downdip at 40-60 km; the 89-day GNSS inversion here finds afterslip up-dip and lateral and none below the rupture, agreeing only on the eastern patch.
disagreements.quote: finding that the majority of afterslip is concentrated downdip of the mainshock between 40-60 km depth

disagreements.target: Coupling-variation stress model of Herman and Furlong (2021)
disagreements.support: Geodetic coupling in the western Semidi segment is only 30±10% (Drooff & Freymueller 2021), not the assumed 100%, so the coupling contribution to shear stress on the M7.6 plane is likely more modest.
disagreements.quote: which is much lower than the 100% assumed by Herman and Furlong (2021)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Direct inversion of wrapped InSAR phase (WGBIS)
alternatives_considered.reason: Incoherence across water channels between islands makes unwrapping ill-posed, with unknown 2π multiples

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Unconstrained or regularized high-dimensional slip distributions (deterministic or Bayesian)
alternatives_considered.reason: Resolution falls with depth and offshore distance; published models agree on smooth slip; finite crack-tip stress; low dimensionality and smaller null space

alternatives_considered.chosen: Joint GNSS and InSAR wrapped-phase inversion
alternatives_considered.reason: Sparse GNSS cannot tightly constrain the geometry

alternatives_considered.chosen: Two-segment geometry (26° deep segment plus shallow segment to the trench)
alternatives_considered.reason: Better InSAR fit and better-resolved posteriors

alternatives_considered.chosen: Postseismic correction of the ascending M7.8 interferogram only
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Correcting the M7.6 interferograms as well
alternatives_considered.reason: No clear M7.6 transient in interferograms or GNSS, and M7.8 postseismic signal negligible by then

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Other smoothing factors along the trade-off curve; compact elliptical model for afterslip
alternatives_considered.reason: Trade-off curve between misfit and roughness; afterslip unlikely to be compact

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Two segments including a shallow trench-parallel segment
alternatives_considered.reason: Two-segment geodetic inversions are not stable

alternatives_considered.chosen: Kula-Resurrection ridge fabric as the M7.6 source fault
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Outer-rise bending faults; Pacific-Kula ridge fabric; Pacific-Farallon ridge fabric
alternatives_considered.reason: Strike and dip consistency; rival orientations inconsistent
